newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss ties to Nazi Germany need study - historians.
newsitem.headline: Swiss ties to Nazi Germany need study - historians.

text.p: Switzerland's past as a black market for Nazi loot and its importance as a financier to Hitler's war effort is still largely unexplored and must be uncovered, leading Swiss historians said on Tuesday.

Swiss business with the Axis powers surrounding it during World War Two is well doumented, but it remains unclear how much Swiss money and material helped Germany continue its war effort until defeat in 1945, they told a government-sponsored seminar.

Even less clear is the extent to which the Nazis used neutral Switzerland's status as a financial centre untouched by the war to sell or hoard cash, gold, jewels and securities seized from Jews and other victims, they said.
"It is urgent and important that this research be undertaken," said Marc Perrenoud, an expert on Swiss financial relations with Nazi Germany and Mussolini's Italy.
Perrenoud and other top Swiss historians attended the seminar on what is known already and what must be probed in a major historical inquiry the government launched last December.

Perrenoud said while Berne froze German assets in Switzerland near the end of the war under pressure from the Allied powers, it was not clear to him whether all stolen goods had ever been returned to the rightful owners.
"After looking through the Swiss Federal Archives, there is cause to doubt this (return)," he said.

Federal Archives director Christoph Graf said historians had once thought Switzerland's role in financing and supplying the German war effort was marginal, but were increasingly viewing it as a major help for Hitler.

Germany and Italy pressured tiny Switzerland into extending credits during the war, transported strategic supplies such as coal through the Swiss Alps, bought material from Swiss companies and frequently used Swiss banks.
"But the theory that the war lasted two years longer because of Swiss financial and economic assistance is no more than a hypothesis now, although it cannot be dismissed," he said.

Gian Trepp, who has written extensively about German wartime sales of gold it stole from occupied countries' central banks, said one murky area was the movement of other Nazi loot through Switzerland.
Trepp said little was known about the extent to which the German state and individual Nazis used Switzerland as a black market to unload treasures seized from concentration camp prisoners and others.

"It must be assumed that there was a market in Switzerland for stolen gold, jewels, stocks and bonds and so on," he said, noting that Switzerland had intact banks, businesses and bourses and an easily convertible currency during the war.
"This market must be studied. As far as I am aware, this has not been done," he added.

Historians said these and other points would fall under the sweeping probe of wartime history by nine Swiss and international historians named by Berne in December and whose first meeting is set for March 5-8.

Berne commissioned the study, including giving the historians limited power to lift bank secrecy, under pressure led by world Jewish groups for compensation for what they say was Swiss profiteering from the Holocaust.
The political urgency for Berne to uncover dark spots in the Swiss past was underscored by an emotional appeal at the seminar from three Jewish-American Holocaust survivors who are suing Swiss banks.

"I accuse Switzerland of violating my human and civil rights by turning back my beloved father and thousands of other Jewish refugees from the Holocaust," said Sylvia Hinda Fekete, a Belgian-born resident of Brooklyn.

Fekete is part of one of two class-action suits filed in New York seking billions of dollars from Swiss banks for accounts the claimants say were left by Holocaust victims and withheld by the banks from the rightful heirs.
